Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye meet in Islamabad as Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue and Iran talks stay open.

Islamabad, Pakistan – Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are meeting in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their Mecca defence pact, as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and sporadic Iranian strikes on other Gulf countries continue.

The officials are meeting for the third time since the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three.

The agreement was signed amid a wider war that began with United States-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told the AFP news agency earlier this week that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia” – a reference to Yemen, where the Houthis are based – would be on the agenda. He confirmed that the defence and foreign ministers of all three countries would attend the Islamabad meeting.

“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.

He described the pact as still being at an early stage.

“Initially we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he said.

Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but has ruled out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.

A pledge with limits

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs set out that boundary on October 9. Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistani troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance would not cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis.

“It is an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression,” he said at the weekly news briefing.

On April 11, as Islamabad hosted talks between US and Iranian officials aimed at ending the war, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the country’s Eastern Province under a bilateral mutual defence agreement that Islamabad and Riyadh had signed in 2025.

Muhammad Faisal, a Sydney-based security and foreign policy analyst, said much of the Pakistani military presence in Saudi Arabia rested on that older bilateral arrangement.

“Importantly, Pakistan’s existing military presence and defence coordination with Saudi Arabia largely predate the Mecca Pact,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the bilateral mutual defence pact inked in September 2025, at a time when Gulf countries were reevaluating their dependence on US security guarantees after Israel struck Qatar.

Faisal added that Riyadh had not publicly pressed Islamabad to take part in offensive operations inside Yemen.

But Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, said that limit fell short of what Saudi Arabia wanted.

Therein lies a dilemma, both for Pakistan and for Saudi Arabia: The deeper Pakistan becomes involved against the Houthis, Karim said, the weaker its diplomatic role would become in US-Iran mediation and in its more recent efforts to mediate between Iran and Saudi Arabia. That’s because Iran is the principal external backer of the Houthis.

“Saudi Arabia wants Pakistan to contribute to its defence against the Houthis, and perhaps to act more against the Houthis in an offensive manner, but it also wants to retain Pakistan as a conduit of diplomatic engagement with Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pressure on the ground

On November 24, the Saudi Civil Defence said 11 people were injured when a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre was hit in a Houthi attack.

At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.

At an emergency meeting of the pact’s member countries in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.

The joint statement did not name Yemen or the Houthis.

On November 21, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Turkish media: “Our current policy is aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia; no decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia.”

Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based analyst and nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, expected the alliance to remain defensive for the moment.

“As of now, as the Saudis only requested defensive support, I do not expect the Mecca Pact to get involved in offensive military operations against the Houthi militias in Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, outlined the scope of Pakistan’s commitment.

“Pakistan’s military commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia encompasses capabilities across the land and air domains, including combat aviation, ground formations, integrated air and missile defence, and geospatial intelligence support. Defensive military operations can involve direct combat,” he told Al Jazeera.

Building the alliance

The Riyadh meeting was also attended by retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, a former three-star Pakistani general, who was appointed earlier in September as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.

The secretariat is based in Riyadh, where Mahmood met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on November 19 to review efforts to build the alliance’s institutional framework, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.…

India's Modi government calls special sitting of parliament

Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026

The sitting of the Indian parliament comes after its monsoon session was adjourned sine die in August. Follow DW.

What you need to know

These are our rolling updates from India on Friday, November 27:

- A brief sitting of the Indian parliament will take place after the monsoon session was adjourned indefinitely back in August

- India's Lok Sabha is set to meet on Monday

- The Rajya Sabha will resume proceedings on Wednesday

How has india's opposition reacted to the reconvening of parliament?

India's main opposition Congress party has deemed the move by Modi's government to call for the brief sitting of the parliament "an assault on the Constitution of India" which Congress General Secretary in-charge Communications and MP Jairam Ramesh said "must and will be resisted with all might."

In a post on X, Ramesh accused the government of "moving to manufacture a fraudulent two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha"

Ramesh also listed out a three-point Congress stance on delimitation and women's quota, which includes:

- Maintaining the current strength of the Lok Sabha for another 25 years.

- Maintaining the current state-wise distribution of seats in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years

- Implementation of one-third reservation for women and reservation within reservation for women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from the next general elections, slated for 2029.

A meeting of the Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group is also expected to be held on Saturday to discuss the gameplan for the upcoming parliament sitting, news agency ANI reported.

Indian parliament to hold special sitting after a gap of more than 100 days

A political storm could be on the horizon in India as both houses of India's bicameral parliament are set to reconvene next week for a special sitting at the request of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The Lok Sabha (lower house) is slated to sit on November 30 while the Rajya Sabha (upper house) will meet on December 2, official memos said, adding that the session may conclude on December 3.

"The Government has requested Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha and Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026 respectively to transact essential Government Business," Union Minister of Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju wrote on X, announcing the government's request on Thursday evening.

The resumption of parliament comes after the monsoon session, which is the second regular session of India's legislative body, saw both the houses being adjourned sine die (indefinitely) on August 13.

The session never ended formally and has remained unprorogued for a record over 100 days, while a winter session that typically starts early December looks delayed.

The monsoon session was turbulent as it began amid a massive youth-led protest called by India's "Cockroach" movement that sought, and later managed to get, the resignation of Modi's then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.

The parliament, itself, became a protest ground as both Modi's ruling coalition, led by his Bharatiya Janata Party, and the opposition INDIA bloc, by Congress, held demonstrations within its premises.

The political deadlock was unrelenting and the parliament struggled to get much business underway, culminating in the adjournment.

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with your daily dose of news from India.

Here is what's creating a buzz in the world's largest democracy this morning:

Indian lawmakers are making their way back to the parliament next week, more than three months after a rocky — and not formal — conclusion of the monsoon session of the country's supreme legislative body which struggled to conduct its business amid an outpouring of protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over student issues.

The Modi government's request to reconvene both houses of the parliament for a special sitting has been accepted, with parliamentarians huddling in the Lok Sabha — the lower house — on November 30 and Rajya Sabha — the upper house — on December 2.

The ruling coalition has not explicitly stated what affairs it wants to discuss during the short session and has only said it wants to "transact essential government business."

However, speculation is rife that Modi's government could once again push a package of defeated bills — including a contentious population-based redrawing of voting boundaries and a women's quota intertwined with it.

And in the world of cricket, it is day one of the second test match between India and New Zealand in Christchurch's Hagley Oval . Both teams are vying for a series win in this final match after the first one in Wellington ended in a draw.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear context

SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."

"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.

"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."

The company did not respond to a request for comment on the reported job cuts. The number could change after labor negotiations.

Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.

Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.

The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.

Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.

In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.

The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy. This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.

The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

Almost a million Americans left without power on Thanksgiving as storm sweeps East Coast

Nearly a million people were left without power Thursday after a severe storm lashed the East Coast of the US, tearing up trees and powerlines on Thanksgiving. New York City authorities had been forced to postpone the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade due to the intense winds.

A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the US East Coast on Thursday, knocking out power to nearly 1 million customers at one point ‌as wind gusts of up to 112kph toppled trees and power lines.

The storm contributed to flight delays, with FlightAware reporting a total of 454 US-related cancellations on Thursday and 2,411 delays. ‌Major airports in the Washington and New York City areas were among the hardest hit.

Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned of an increased risk of falling trees and power outages.

More than 908,000 US utility customers had no power as of 9:56pm ET (0256 GMT), according to PowerOutage.us, down from 961,000 ‌at 7:30pm ET.

The data included more than 207,000 outages in Pennsylvania, over 179,000 in New Jersey, 139,000 in Maryland, 106,000 in Virginia, 100,000 in Missouri and more than 68,000 in New York state.

Wind ‌gusts of 80 to 112kph were reported or forecast across parts of Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York, and coastal New England, according to the US National Weather Service.

It said conditions would gradually improve across the Mid-Atlantic overnight as the heaviest rain and strongest winds moved into New England, although blustery conditions with gusts of 40 to 55kph were expected across parts of the East Coast on Friday.

New York City Emergency Management reported winds intensified on Thursday afternoon, reaching 90kph at LaGuardia Airport.

The NWS said strong onshore winds associated with the storm, combined with king tides, were causing coastal flooding in low-lying communities along portions of the East Coast.

Officials had already postponed Thursday's 100th edition of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City because of the storm threat, the first time the event has been rescheduled due to severe weather.

People were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.

“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said.

Separately on Thursday, US President Donald Trump said he had approved about $100 million in federal aid to Florida following severe storms and flooding there. He said the total included funding previously approved in connection with Hurricane Isaias.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AP)

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear context

Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?

The presumptive House speaker’s political pragmatism will be tested by divisions over healthcare, Israel and the war on Iran.

The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as a crowning achievement for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries that propelled him into the position of next speaker of the House of Representatives. And while that outcome appears all but guaranteed now that he has secured more than enough support from the incoming House Democratic Caucus, Jeffries’ ascent to the top House leadership position has been significantly rockier than anticipated.

The blue wave was, in part, a progressive and anti-establishment phenomenon. And while we in the media have likely exaggerated the impact of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in this year’s election cycle, DSA-affiliated and other newly elected far-left lawmakers have already asserted themselves as a vocal minority amongst the incoming House Democratic Caucus. They’ve done so by calling on the party to move left on issues such as healthcare, campaign finance and America’s relationship with Israel. And these newly elected progressives have also targeted congressional leaders, namely Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who they see as embodying the party’s status quo.

Jeffries has reached the pinnacle of power within his party by being a shrewd political operator who has deftly managed the leverage of the Democratic minority in the closely divided House. His handling of the recent challenge to his leadership shows that he remains a step ahead of his opponents within the party. Jeffries declined the opportunity to be chosen by acclamation, an option that could have allowed him to gloss over the opposition to his speakership. Instead, Jeffries insisted on a formal secret ballot. The choice was strategic. Much like a prime minister calling for early elections, he organised the vote to happen before progressive opposition had coalesced around a single candidate (unlike in the Senate, where Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen is amassing support to challenge Schumer). The move represented a tactic Jeffries observed while under the wing of Nancy Pelosi, who called a similar vote in 2018 after her leadership was challenged by vocal incoming members of Congress. In the end, potential challengers for the role of speaker, such as Representatives Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, declined to throw their hats in the ring to run against Jeffries. The vast majority of the caucus fell in line behind the New York congressman, with 251 votes in favour and only 11 against, the latter largely from incoming DSA-aligned representatives-elect.

For Jeffries, the progressive revolt against his leadership has been, in the short term, a mere speed bump on his path to becoming speaker. In the longer term, those 11 “no” votes represent a more significant progressive challenge to Jeffries’ record and agenda that will not easily disappear. However, the presumptive next speaker of the House is poised to overcome this challenge, as his skill as a political operative, the relatively weak position of his progressive opposition, and the historic nature of Jeffries’ leadership all work in his favour.

Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Jeffries secured the support of important progressive figures, including fellow New Yorkers such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. During the brief post-election speculation over his leadership, the New York congressman also won over progressives including Texas Representative Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Jeffries’ predecessor as Democratic leader, Pelosi, was able to manage dissent from the progressive Squad through a combination of personal relationships and strategic committee assignments that channelled their energies toward oversight of the executive branch. Jeffries may likewise seek to manage the “Bloc”, as the new progressives are being called by some, in similar fashion.

Meanwhile, Jeffries’ primary message since the midterm elections has been one of affordability, a potent message that has resonated with voters across the political spectrum and thus can unite centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. The speaker-designate has also signalled that he is willing to move in the direction of progressives’ concerns on substantive issues. Most notably, on November 17, the eve of the speaker nomination vote, Jeffries endorsed a plan to expand Medicare by lowering the age of eligibility for older Americans, covering children under 18, and including dental, vision and hearing coverage. This new “Medicare for more” plan, coupled with rolling back Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits, has been gaining steam among both centrists and progressives. The latter have framed it as a quickly achievable first step towards Medicare for All. Both progressive elder statesman Senator Bernie Sanders and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus have adopted this rhetoric.

Whether this “first step” framing is accurate is unknowable. The Affordable Care Act was presented in similar terms, but the progressive aim to use Obamacare as a foundation to build a universal healthcare system did not materialise over the subsequent decade. However, the willingness of major progressive forces to adopt the narrative seems to be opening space for Jeffries to navigate. This undercuts the power that the incoming progressives have to make healthcare a major dividing issue within the Democratic caucus.…

Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state

The takeover of Palestinian homes in Jericho exposes the futility of sanctions that leave Israel’s settler-colonial system intact.

On November 17, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda Fheidat, was shot in the head and killed as she stood outside her home in al-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho. Fadda was murdered by Israeli settlers, who had recently forcibly evicted at least 13 Palestinian households from their homes in the neighbourhood.

What makes this takeover so significant is the location: the outskirts of Jericho, widely described as the world’s oldest continuously inhabited city and the first city to be handed over to the newly established Palestinian Authority in 1994 following the Oslo Accords.

Hours after Fadda was killed, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich visited the new settlement outpost and praised the settlers for what he characterised as a renewal of Jewish settlement in Jericho. It is the first Israeli settlement established inside a Palestinian city in the West Bank since settlers established a presence in the heart of Hebron nearly five decades ago.

This latest settler takeover was spearheaded by the far-right settler organisation Nachala with the support of the settler Binyamin Regional Council. Nachala was founded by the fanatical settler Daniella Weiss and has long campaigned for the ethnic cleansing and settlement of all of historic Palestine. Weiss and her organisation have gained international notoriety as a result of their relentless campaign calling for the Israeli government to complete the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and settle the area with Israelis.

Albeit politically significant, the takeover of homes in Jericho is not surprising. Since the genocide in Gaza began more than three years ago, Israeli settler takeover of Palestinian homes and land has drastically escalated in the West Bank. More than 6,000 Palestinians – half of whom are children – have been forcibly expelled as a result. The Israeli military has also been conducting its own expulsions. Between January and February 2025, the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps in the northern West Bank were emptied of their populations – some 33,000 residents.

One cannot separate the actions of the settlers and the military. The two work hand in glove towards their ultimate goal, which is to force as many Palestinians as possible off the land.

Both actors are part of a larger settler-colonial structure which enables this accelerating expansion. Indeed, the majority of settlements in the West Bank are connected to Israeli regime infrastructure, including Israeli-only roads and water and electricity networks, and many offer state subsidies as incentives for Jewish Israelis to live there. When one sees the settlements with one’s own eyes, it is clear that there is no separation between them and the Israeli state.

Yet the distinction between settlers and the settler-colonial structure is a useful tool for Israel’s more liberal supporters. To blame the settlers and a few more extreme ministers is to provide a scapegoat for the structure that masquerades as the only liberal democracy in the region.

We can see this scapegoating in how some Western governments have responded to settlement expansion. For example, both Nachala and Weiss have been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada and the European Union – sanctions that include asset freezes and travel bans. Sanctions like this effectively allow governments to claim action, when in reality, the impact on the ground is limited.

This distinction between settlers and the Israeli regime is also evident in the language used to announce the sanctions. In her November 18 statement announcing the sanctions, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong failed to mention the Israeli government at all: “We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution”.

Some might argue that freezing settler assets and imposing travel bans is at least a step in the right direction. But this is a naive outlook. Limited sanctions like these are a politically calculated tactic. In the UK, growing anger among the British public over their government’s complicity in the genocide necessitated a response from the incoming prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Yet when his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced earlier this year the new approach the UK government was taking vis-à-vis Palestine and Israel, it was reported that British officials were also working to de-escalate tensions and give assurances to the Israeli government that the sanctions would be limited in scope.

Indeed, the earlier sanctions did nothing to stop what happened in al-Duyuk at-Tahta, where Palestinians were evicted from their homes by settlers, supported by soldiers and praised by government ministers. In fact, the settler movement appears to be intact and growing in support and power every day.

This is why sanctions cannot be limited to individual actors and organisations – they need to be comprehensively applied to the structure behind them. But that requires a moral backbone and political courage – something that seems to be completely lacking on the international stage.

item.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear context

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.

He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit on Thursday. The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.

De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.

He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.

Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.

Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.

De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.

Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.

Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.

Not a dove, not a hawk, but an 'owl'

Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.

That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.

De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.

"It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments.

- Date:

Zhejiang University

- Summary:

Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

- Share:

Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

Two Ages Stand Out for Screen Time Risks

The researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

One possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

"The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters."

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

An additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

The researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. - Summary:

Harvard-led researchers have developed a microscopic device that generates 120 times more ultraviolet light than previous comparable approaches by efficiently converting red light into UV. The breakthrough could unlock smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and compact environmental sensors.

- Share:

Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Turning Red Light Into Ultraviolet Light

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet."

A New Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

Previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling."

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy."

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

The team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

A 120-Fold Increase in Ultraviolet Power

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.…

Rather than preparing and testing each candidate catalyst individually, the research team, led by Professor Paul Lusby from the University of Edinburgh, developed a rapid screening approach allowing cages to be assembled and assessed immediately in solution. Co-author Dr. Jamie Lewis, an expert in cages and Royal Society university research fellow at the University of Birmingham, said, "Traditionally, discovering better cage catalysts has relied heavily on laborious trial-and-error experimentation and computationally expensive modeling. DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space

Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. To better represent what happens on these surfaces, astrophysicists at the University of Liège are proposing a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not yet been utilized in astrochemistry. The paper is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Research in astrochemistry is organized into several branches. Astronomers measure molecular abundances using telescopes, laboratories replicate the conditions of the interstellar medium to study physical and chemical processes, and theoretical chemists focus on specific molecules or reactions. Kinetic models (models that calculate how the quantities of different molecules change over time, based on the rate at which the processes that create or destroy them occur) bridge the gap between these approaches. They use parameters derived from experiments and calculations to predict abundances, which are then compared with observations.

Infrared spectra recently obtained by the James Webb Space Telescope confirm that the chemistry on the surface of the grains and the resulting population of species are extremely complex, making it necessary to incorporate this chemistry more realistically into the models.

"On a grain, the chemistry results from a delicate balance between adsorption—when molecules from the gas settle on the surface—and a series of surface processes such as diffusion or encounters between reaction partners, as well as desorption, when molecules leave the grain to return to the gaseous phase," explain Maria Groyne and Cedric Baijot, FNRS Ph.D. students supervised by Michaël De Becker, an astrophysicist and director of the MEGA Laboratory at ULiège. "The deterministic models published to date already describe these mechanisms, but at the cost of two significant approximations."

The first concerns the surface itself. In the extremely cold conditions of the interstellar medium, the ice covering the grains is not crystalline but amorphous. Its surface is disordered and offers binding sites of varying strength depending on the local environment. Most models, however, assign only a single binding energy to each chemical species. The second approximation relates to interactions between molecules: in the standard formalism, two species present on the surface only influence each other when they react. Yet a simple encounter can alter the strength with which a molecule is bound to the surface.

"The DESTINY model, which we have developed entirely from scratch, overcomes these two simplifications," explains Baijot, an FNRS Ph.D. student at ULiège. "The model classifies surface sites according to their binding energy and, in a deterministic manner, tracks the possible path of each adsorbed species. At each stage, the species may remain in place, diffuse to another site, react with a partner or leave the surface. Markov chains with absorbing states enable these competing outcomes to be handled in a consistent manner."

Like on a dance floor

The researchers use the image of a dance floor to illustrate their approach. In classical models, all the tiles on the floor are identical, and the molecules—which play the role of dancers—behave in the same way everywhere. Two dancers who meet and dance together represent a chemical reaction.

"With DESTINY, the dance floor becomes uneven," explains Groyne, an FNRS Ph.D. student. "Some tiles are sticky, others slippery, and two identical dancers may meet different fates depending on where they are. The mere presence of another dancer can also alter the possible movements, without any reaction taking place. This is the case with dihydrogen: an encounter between two H₂ molecules can set one of them in motion, or even eject it into the gaseous phase."

Initial analyses show that the population of a single species is distributed across sites with varying energy levels, which influences surface chemistry. The team considers the trends observed for methane to be encouraging compared with previous models. These results will need to be investigated further. "This opens a new door to deterministic astrochemical modeling in the solid phase," emphasizes De Becker, "with prospects that we are only just beginning to explore."

This work is primarily fundamental research. It aims to improve our understanding of the chemistry of the interstellar medium and, in the longer term, to shed light on questions such as the origin of molecules associated with life or the complexity of molecules that may form elsewhere in the universe. "Because it describes chemistry on solid and irregular surfaces, the model could also, in the long term, be applied to other environments, such as natural aerosols present in Earth's atmosphere or that of Mars," conclude the study's authors. This avenue remains to be explored.

A Markov chain describes something that transitions randomly from one state to another, following a simple rule: the probability of the next step depends only on the current state, not on the path taken to reach it. The Game of the Goose is a good example. At each turn, the square you land on depends on the roll of the dice and the square you are currently on. Squares visited previously do not matter. Each square is a "state," and the dice determine the probabilities of moving from one state to another. This is known as "memorylessness": the present is sufficient to predict the future.

An absorbing state is one from which you can never escape. In the Game of the Goose, this is the finishing square: once reached, the game is over. These chains allow us to calculate the probability of ending up in each of the final outcomes, and how many steps it takes on average to get there.

Researchers have engineered a ‘molecular glue’ that can stabilize chromosomes in ageing mouse eggs1. They say their artificial cohesion system could pave the way for improved fertility treatments for women over the age of 35.

Chromosomes in animal eggs are held together by protein structures called cohesins. These help to ensure that chromosomes divide correctly during the process of cell division. But the level of cohesins declines as women age, which can cause chromosomes to separate early and be distributed incorrectly. The resulting eggs can have too many or too few chromosomes, a condition known as aneuploidy, which is a cause of infertility, failed in-vitro-fertilization (IVF) treatments and early pregnancy loss, particularly in women who are more than 35 years old.

To prevent this premature separation of chromosomes in eggs, Melina Schuh, a biochemist at Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, and her colleagues designed an artificial system called TALhesin. The system uses engineered proteins that attach to regions of the chromosome in which cohesin is usually present, these proteins then bind to one another.

Many groups are trying to understand cohesin because it diminishes as women age, affecting fertility, says Bettina Mihalas, a reproductive biologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, but this is the first approach to replace the protein’s function with an engineered system. “It’s a very creative, well-engineered and well-thought-out approach,” she says.

The findings were published in Science on 26 November.

Genetic instructions

The researchers injected messenger RNA that encoded the engineered proteins into immature mouse eggs. The mouse eggs then produced the proteins. Using fluorescence microscopy imaging, the researchers confirmed that the TALhesin proteins attached to chromosome regions in which natural cohesin is normally lost.

In 17-month-old mice, the proportion of eggs without any premature chromosome-separation errors increased from 46.7% to 74.1% in those treated with TALhesin, similar to what is observed in eggs from young mice.

Chromatids — the two identical halves formed by a replicating chromosome — must separate at the right time during cell division. To enable this, the researchers added a ‘molecular scissor’ into their artificial system. This switched off the artificial cohesion system at the appropriate time.

Human chromosomes

The team have adapted the system to deliver engineered proteins that attach to regions of human chromosomes in which cohesin is usually present.

Experiments in donated human eggs showed that the TALhesin proteins accumulated in these regions. The researchers also found that chromosomes with high levels of the engineered proteins tended to have smaller distances between chromatids. This demonstrates that the TALhesin system holds the chromosomes together.

For most of October, parts of Indonesia felt dystopian as wildfires turned the sky a reddish orange.

“It felt like you were on Mars,” says Erin Vogel, a primatologist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

Vogel was visiting the Tuanan Orangutan Research Station in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, at the time. She and her colleagues have been conducting research on the critically endangered Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) there for more than 20 years, but this trip she spent much of her time fighting fires. There were roughly 300,000 blazes in the region between July and October, and October’s level of toxic particulate matter in the air was roughly 400 times higher than what the World Health Organization deems safe.

Indonesia is experiencing one of its most severe fire and haze season of the past three decades, in part because a super El Niño has dried out vegetation and brought winds that fuelled the flames. More than 2.8 million hectares have burnt across Indonesia so far, and Kalimantan has been affected the worst. Fires devoured 60% of Bornean orangutans’ habitats in Kalimantan, including healthy forests such as those at the Tuanan research station and in Gunung Palung National Park.

Nature spoke to Vogel about the disaster and what it means for orangutans. At the time of the interview, fires were still smouldering in Tuanan peat swamp forests.

What was it like at the Tuanan research station during the peak?

It was depressing and horrid. I’ve never seen so much forest loss in the 23 years I have worked in Indonesia. In the sky, there was this orange-brown haze that was very thick and it burnt your lungs if you weren’t wearing a respirator.

When I arrived in Tuanan, it really struck me how quiet the forests had become. You didn’t hear birds; you didn’t hear insects; you didn’t hear anything except trees burning and falling.

The forest staff, the orangutan staff, the phenology staff and the fire teams were all fighting fires. I felt in awe of those heroes voluntarily fighting these fires day and night. They’d all been doing so for more than two months straight. It takes real strength to be able to do that and not give up, and our team is just so positive and hopeful.

How have the fires affected the orangutans?

We saw some orangutans who seemed to be very lethargic and sick. We came across one of the males we’ve been studying for more than 15 years, and he was on the ground, breathing heavily. But when we saw him a couple of days later, he seemed to have recovered a little bit. He was near the research station, eating some vegetation on the ground, climbing trees and eating fruits. That reassures us that he is doing better.

We’re seeing orangutans being displaced from one area to others. That means we’re going to have competition between individuals over limited resources. That’s also going to change their behaviour. It’s going to be interesting to see what happens.

Genomic work helps find treatment for rare blood disorder

Sisters with a rare blood condition are the first patients to receive a repurposed drug to treat it, after a team of doctors and cardiovascular scientists used genomic sequencing to identify the drug's target.

The research, which includes findings from the successful treatment in two adult sisters living in the West Midlands in the U.K., is published in the Blood Journal. The work was led by professor Neil Morgan from the University of Birmingham, Dr. Manoj Raghavan from University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust and Dr. Hrushikesh Vyas, who carried out laboratory tests as part of his Ph.D. at the University of Birmingham.

The condition is called SRC-related thrombocytopenia, which is a very rare disorder that causes a gene to constantly express a protein involved in platelet production and activation. Patients have abnormally low levels of platelets and often develop an enlarged spleen, immune issues and scarring in their bone marrow where blood cells are made. Existing treatment options have largely focused on supplementing low platelets through blood transfusions, which require regular hospital trips.

Following work to understand the mechanism involved in SRC-related thrombocytopenia using genetic testing, the team was able to identify that dasatinib, used in blood cancer treatment, could dampen down the SRC protein's activity and help patients have more typical platelet production by reversing the bone marrow damage.

Morgan, from the University of Birmingham and lead author of the study, said, "Advances in genomics have meant we have been able to identify how an existing drug used in cancer therapy can treat this specific rare blood condition. The findings themselves have already made a difference for these patients, but also show the way forward using genomics to identify how medicines already in use can make a difference for the many rare diseases and conditions that currently aren't treatable.

"The work which has changed the sisters' day-to-day lives is thanks to the close working between the university and hospital through Birmingham Health Partners and Cancer Research UK."

Raghavan, a consultant hematologist from University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust who treated the two sisters, said, "This is a lovely example of how translational research can transform patients' lives. Genomics identified a mutation that we were able to target by repurposing a drug usually used to treat a type of leukemia. Even though this is a rare condition, it gives an insight into how the bone marrow works that can be taken forward for other blood diseases."

It's great now—although I never stopped traveling. Manjit's story

Since starting the treatment around three years ago, dasatinib has helped Manjit Kaur improve her blood counts and stop needing transfusions. Now, Kaur has felt less tired and has been able to continue her two passions—traveling and working in her local health center.

Kaur began taking dasatinib after her sister, who has the same condition, responded well to the treatment. After starting on the drug and working out the right amount for her alongside her Crohn's disease, Kaur now takes a dose she can manage and has regular blood tests at hospital every three months. Her blood counts have improved, and she no longer needs transfusions.

"I mean, I've never let it stop me doing anything," Kaur says. "I've always carried on working and traveling. But it's great to not have to go in (to hospital) for regular transfusions."

Kaur, who lives in the West Midlands, was diagnosed with SRC in 1989, in her late teens or early 20s. She believes she may have had the condition for several years before it was identified. At the time, she often felt tired and bruised easily, but thought the symptoms were part of living with Crohn's disease, which she had been diagnosed with as a child.

Her childhood was shaped by hospital visits and time away from school. She was treated in Wolverhampton, at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London and later in Birmingham. Kaur missed many lessons and left school without sitting her final exams.

She later completed training courses, gained qualifications and built a career in administration. For the past 31 years, she has worked as an IT administrator at a general practitioner's office, where she also completed a foundation degree in information and communication technologies.

Kaur hopes her experience will encourage others to consider taking part in clinical trials or trying a treatment offered to them. "Give it a go," she says. "If it doesn't work, you can stop. And you're helping other people, because doctors can learn what works for others too."

When is it time to treat obesity? An expert explains it's not just a lack of willpower

If you're trying to figure out how to treat obesity, the choices can feel overwhelming. Diet plans, weight-loss surgery, newer pills and weekly injections all promise results, and it's hard to know when and where to start.

HealthDay sat down for an exclusive interview with Dr. Rachel Batterham, senior vice president of cardiometabolic health at Eli Lilly and Co., at the health care innovation conference HLTH USA 2026 in Las Vegas.

She talked about why lost weight is so hard to keep off and how to choose a treatment that fits your life.

Her first message: Obesity isn't a failure of willpower.

"For many years people just viewed obesity as a lifestyle choice," Batterham said. "I can promise you nobody would choose to have severe obesity."

For most of human history, food was scarce, she explained, so the body is wired to eat whenever food is around. Today, people are surrounded by food cues. And when you diet, your body treats it like a famine.

"They can lose the weight," Batterham said. "But then the biology kicks in to fight against it."

So what should you consider when thinking about obesity treatments?

Batterham suggests starting with lifestyle basics, such as cutting back on ultraprocessed foods and looking at physical activity, stress and sleep.

The next question is whether extra weight is affecting your health.

Where you carry it matters, she said. Weight around the belly is more closely tied to high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and heart disease than weight in other places. A family history of those conditions or of severe obesity also raises the stakes.

"It really comes down to what's the health outcome, not necessarily the numbers on the scale," she said.

For years, Batterham led a bariatric surgery center in the U.K. to treat people struggling with obesity.

"One of the things about bariatric surgery is that from the moment you have the surgery, then your appetite is completely reduced," she said.

She explained that after surgery, hormones like GLP-1s go up and this helps drive the marked weight loss after the procedure.

This hormone connection is how newer obesity medications entered the treatment landscape.

Anyone considering medication should know it's likely to be a lifelong treatment, Batterham added. Stopping usually means regaining the weight, much like blood pressure climbs again when someone quits blood pressure pills.

There's no one-size-fits-all option, she said. Someone who travels often, for example, may prefer a pill over carrying an injection pen.

Batterham walks patients through the choices and expected benefits, then often asks them to talk it over with loved ones, since the whole household is involved.

Most of today's drugs are GLP-1 medicines, which mimic a gut hormone that curbs appetite.

They aren't right for everyone. Stomach and gut side effects are the most common, so people who already have digestive problems should be cautious. The drugs can't be used during pregnancy, so women hoping to conceive need careful planning.

Raising the dose too fast can cause nausea, diarrhea or constipation, so slower is often better, Batterham said. Patients also need enough protein and fluids.

However, with the right support and instructions, she said, "patients tend to do very well."

'We feed and wash her': Severe ME leaves woman bedbound for five years

Rowena Davies had been planning to travel the world with her partner until an ME diagnosis left her unable to talk or leave her bed.

The 42-year-old, known as Row, initially thought she was burnt out, but after years of searching for answers was finally diagnosed in 2021 and her partner Shauna Chambers has since given up work to help the family care for her.

Campaigners are warning that people with severe ME - sometimes referred to clinically as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome - could die without changes to services in Wales.

The Welsh government said proposals for an allâWales specialist, an expert group and national standards were being considered.

It is estimated more than 400,000 people across the UK have ME, a complex multi-system condition with no known cure.

Shauna, 34, said: "She had a cough that didn't leave for many months, but the main thing was that she would be absolutely drained and exhausted after doing such small things.

"Now, she really isn't able to do anything at all."

Shauna, from Tywyn in Gwynedd, said Row was "full of energy" and loved sport, but now she cannot tolerate light or noise, and any exertion will cause her to deteriorate.

"We feed her, we wash her, we brush her teeth. We were left to navigate this on our own," she said.

"It's like you're grieving someone that is still alive, and you sit next to her sometimes, and all you can do is just hold her hand and breathe.

"People's lives have been completely ruined by this condition, and if nothing changes people can die from ME, and it is absolutely avoidable."

Campaigners told BBC Wales in March that healthcare services were "like a desert" for those most severely affected.

With the right support, Row's family are hopeful she can get better. She recently had her first visit by the Living Well service within Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which has been expanded to include ME, and now aims to support people living with any severity of the condition.

It uses funding from the Welsh government's Adferiad programme, external but campaigners say that services vary between health boards. There is no clinical lead for ME in Wales.

John Peters, 65, from Swansea, was diagnosed with the condition 40 years ago. He was once a keen rugby player, but after a virus, his life changed.

"I've gone through improvements, and then got another infection, and that's been the cycle of my life since 1985," he said.

"One of the hardest things is the loss of identity. You're not a husband, a father, you don't have a career.

"Your life goes past and then you realise what's happened. I hate the illness.

"No one knows what I've been through. There is no care for me."

Swansea Bay University Health Board said its service, also funded by the Adferiad programme, "focuses on improving quality of life, supporting independence, and enabling individuals to manage the impact of ME within their own daily circumstances" while "recognising the fluctuating nature of the condition and the importance of personalised care".

What is myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME)?

ME is a chronic and complex multi-system condition, which causes symptoms such as extreme fatigue and post-exertional malaise.

That means simple physical or mental activities can leave people completely debilitated.

Not everyone with ME is affected in the same way. There is a spectrum of severity, which is often categorised as mild, moderate, severe and very severe.

While researchers are still investigating the causes, triggers may include infection or other illness. There is no specific treatment.

Source: NHS

'People do die from severe ME'

Liverpool-based private consultant Dr Binita Kane, who has a special interest in ME and long Covid, said she had a growing waiting list of patients across the UK.

"I think that is a sad reflection on the fact that the services, sadly, don't exist at the moment in the way they need to through the NHS," she said.

"Even if patients can access a service, they often can't access medications and treatments for symptom control and support for overlapping conditions because there aren't doctors integrated into those services."

She said the goal is always "to prevent people from getting into the very severe state" through early intervention, but she said that certain investigations can happen at people's homes, such as 24-hour ECG tests, sleep studies and blood tests.

"People sadly do die from severe ME for different reasons, it is a risk, and ME is one of the only conditions I'm aware of where the more sick you are, the less access to treatment and help and support you get," she added.

"These are young people whose lives have been decimated, destroyed, who aren't getting enough help, care, and support.

"There's a million reasons why the government should be taking this extremely seriously."

Campaign groups in Wales have joined together to call on the government to bring together a national expert group, appoint an all-Wales clinical lead, and develop a research strategy.

In a recent survey of more than 5,400 people across the UK, 62.1% of respondents in Wales reported having no NHS specialist ME service in their area, compared with 32.8% in England.

Action for ME, who conducted the survey, said the findings demonstrate that "access to specialist care remains a postcode lottery".

"People have been waiting for decades and that is too long" said the charity's chief executive Sonya Chowdhury.

She said that a cross-party debate was held in the Senedd in December 2025 in which the current health minister, Plaid Cymru's Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, advocated on behalf of ME patients while in opposition.

"We are 12 months on, and we are yet to see action," she added.

"It's fantastic that the minister has met with us and other groups here in Wales, and we have heard some positive noises, but what we need to see now is something changing."…

The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline

After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.

He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.

"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."

Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.

Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.

Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.

Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.

"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.

"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.

'Grounding'

Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".

"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.

After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.

"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."

She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.

Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".

Friendship flux

In this episode, you’ll hear two conversations recorded live at We Are Developers. TRANSCRIPT

Ryan Donovan: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Stack Overflow podcast, a place to talk all things software and technology. This episode is a two-parter — conversations recorded at the We Are Developers Conference. First up is a conversation with Ivan Burazin of Daytona, all about sandboxes and portable compute. And after that, a conversation with Richard Risk of Blackbox AI about secure inference. Enjoy.

Today we are talking about all those pesky rogue agents breaking out of their sandboxes, and what we can do to keep them from going rogue. My guest for that is Ivan Burazin, the CEO and co-founder of Daytona. Welcome to the show.

Ivan Burazin: Thank you so much for having me.

Ryan Donovan: So this breaking-out-of-the-sandbox idea has been very much in the news with the Hugging Face attack. What does this mean for the sandboxed methodology of protecting agents from doing whatever they want?

Ivan Burazin: Sure. So I mean, it was all over the news, and rightfully so that people are interested in this. Just one step before I get to that — the sense of the term "sandbox." We at Daytona are a sandbox vendor, as are many other companies. As of yesterday, three more. That's a lot of people doing sandboxes. That being said, sandboxes are both what we like to say "computers for agents" — an actual tool for agents to get things done — but also at the same time, a place where you sort of lock down the agent from other things, hence the name sandbox. It's essentially a secured virtual machine.

Ryan Donovan: It's a VM.

Ivan Burazin: It's essentially a VM. I mean, it could be a container, it could be a VM, it could be a bare metal machine. You could do different variations. The vast majority are virtual machines, or micro-VMs to be more specific. Now, in this case, the Hugging Face attack — it is used for performance reasons, but it's also used for security reasons. Some vendors are security-first sandboxes, so their purpose is to secure the agent. Others, like us, the purpose is to give the agent tools and be as performant as possible. Of course, security is table stakes, but there are different levels to security. So for this specific breakout, the agent escaped the sandbox and was able to access the internet.

I have a few problems with the entire case. One: if you have an agent that has the capability to escape and has no guardrails, it would make sense that you would first put the same model and/or agent with guardrails to test it out.

Ryan Donovan: Well, my understanding of the attack is that this was sort of what they wanted to do. I understood it to be deliberately lowered security. They were doing an exploit benchmark test and they gave it an impossible task.

Ivan Burazin: Yeah, understood. And then, in that case, it should be no surprise that they did it, right? It should be like, oh, it actually did it — great, fine, done. Maybe they could have picked somewhere else, I mean, this was benign, even the break-in of Hugging Face, but they could have picked a random place that they had set up themselves so they didn't go to third parties. So there are conspiracy theories that this was just good marketing or not. But on the other hand, we internally — as one of these companies — every single day, we have multiple companies that we have actually hired to find vulnerabilities in our system, both human and AI, and they find them every day.

The interesting part is that we, as are many other people in this entire ecosystem — not just sandboxes — are built on other projects as well, not just open source projects. And quite recently, there was a new exploit someone found, but it was in the underlying isolation layer that was not ours. And the code — that could have been found five years ago, seven years ago — no one found it. So the interesting thing is that things are being found now that are not necessarily net-new issues, but rather old issues that we have built on. So I think that speaks to what we will have to do as a society in terms of how we update, patch, and actually deploy net-new software or software infrastructure in this new world.

Ryan Donovan: Yeah. I mean, when Mythos was first released, they talked about finding bugs in basically everything that has ever existed as software. I asked somebody who works with the OWASP team, and I was like, what do you think of that? And she said, people are bad at security coding. Do you think that applies to sandboxing code too?

Ivan Burazin: So I would say I'm sure it does in general, but the interesting part is that most sandbox providers are built on either QEMU, Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor, Docker, or gVisor — right on top of those. And then you have the sandbox providers that have their own layers of security on top of their own software. So it is not only a question of whether the sandbox layer is secure, but also whether the underlying isolation is secure. And so then you have multiple vectors of attack or vulnerabilities.…

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Most FYP database chapters fall apart in the viva for one simple reason: the student drew an ERD that looks nice, then built whatever tables felt right in phpMyAdmin.

Here is the order that survives questioning, using a hostel management system as the example:

1. Entities come from the problem statement, not from screens.

Read your problem statement and underline the nouns your system must remember: Student, Room, Allotment, Payment, Complaint. If a noun never gets stored, it is not an entity. If it gets stored and changes over time, it probably is.

2. Draw the ERD before you create a single table.

For each pair of entities, write the relationship in a sentence: "One Room has many Allotments over time, but one Allotment belongs to exactly one Room." That sentence gives you cardinality, and cardinality tells you where the foreign key lives. Panels ask about relationships far more than about box shapes.

3. Normalise to 3NF on paper, in this order.

- 1NF: no repeating groups. A student row with phone1, phone2, phone3 fails this instantly.

- 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. In an Allotment table with a composite key (student_id, room_id), the student's name depends only on student_id — it moves out.

- 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Room rent depends on room type, not on the room number — so rent lives in a RoomType table, not repeated on every Room row.

4. Only now open MySQL.

Create tables in dependency order (the "one" side first), add foreign keys with the right ON DELETE behaviour, and seed each table with 5-10 realistic rows. Realistic data is what makes your demo and your test cases believable.

5. Write the viva answers while you design.

For every table, one sentence: "This table exists because…" If you cannot finish that sentence, the table is either missing or should not exist. This is also exactly the justification your Chapter 3 needs — the full chapter structure (methodology choice, use case diagram, DFD levels, and this database design sequence) is laid out in this Chapter 3 guide if you are writing yours now.

Design on paper first, and the database stops being the scary part of the viva.

Are you drawing your ERD before or after building your tables? I am curious how other students were taught this.
