item.title: Avoiding Partially Written Export Files in GBase 8a with Python UDFs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP database from GBASE, can export over ftp and sftp. When the export is large — tens of GB — the target file takes time to finish writing. If a downstream job picks it up mid-export, it reads an incomplete file, which shows up as inconsistent data or parse errors. This post uses Python UDFs to add ftp / sftp rename support so the file only becomes visible when it is complete.

The idea

Downstream consumers usually scan for files matching a rule, for example *.csv under a load directory. Making an unfinished file fail that rule can be done two ways, and they can be combined:

-

Name does not match — target is .csv, temporary file is .csv.tmp

- Path does not match — write to a temporary directory first

Two steps

- Export to a temporary file (different suffix, or a temporary directory).

- Once the export finishes, use the protocol's rename to switch the temporary name to the final one — changing the suffix or moving across directories.

FTP rename UDF

Stored under gclusterdb, taking host, username, password, source name, target name. Port customisation is not implemented; extend it if you are not on the default ftp port:

use gclusterdb;

drop function if exists ftpRename;

create function ftpRename(server varchar(100),username varchar(100),password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))

returns varchar

$$

from ftplib import FTP

ftp = FTP(server)

ftp.login(username, password)

ftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)

ftp.close()

return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

Calling it:

gbase> select ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| ftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

SFTP rename UDF

The standard Python library does not speak sftp, so this example uses pysftp (pip install pysftp). Everything else matches the FTP version:

use gclusterdb;

drop function if exists sftpRename;

create function sftpRename(server varchar(100),v_username varchar(100),v_password varchar(100),sourceFilename varchar(1000),targetFilename varchar(1000))

returns varchar

$$

import pysftp

with pysftp.Connection(server, username=v_username, password=v_password) as sftp:

sftp.rename(sourceFilename,targetFilename)

sftp.close()

return 'OK'

$$ language plpythonu;

gbase> select sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv');

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1.csv') |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.08)

The full flow

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';

Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.32)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv');

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/t1.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/tmp/t1.csv') |

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.43)

The temporary file can live in a different directory, provided the account has write permission there. This example uses both a temporary tmp directory and a .tmp suffix:

gbase> select * from t1 into outfile 'sftp://gbase:gbase1234@10.0.2.201/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp' fields terminated by ',';

Query OK, 3 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

gbase> select gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv');

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| gclusterdb.sftprename('10.0.2.201','gbase','gbase1234','/home/gbase/tmp/t1_2.csv.tmp','/home/gbase/t1_2.csv') |

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

| OK |

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.44)

Both the export and the rename run inside the gbase client, and the consumer's scan rule never matches a .tmp file. Handing atomic visibility to rename means even a tens-of-GB export no longer needs a sleep timer or a human "is it done yet" check — a small UDF turns the database's own export into a safe handoff.

Step by step

How it works (0:00)

In the next ten minutes, you'll build a real products manager inside your own Shopify app. You'll see the price trap that catches almost every beginner, search your products, and load the next page, with the GraphQL Admin API, and create, edit and delete them, live on a real store. I type a product, give it a price, and it's created in my store through the GraphQL Admin API. This is episode two of the Shopify app development series. Episode one created this app; today it gets its first real feature.

First, the big picture, because every feature in this series follows the same path. Our page is built with Polaris web components. When it needs data, it asks the loader.

When you click save, it calls the action. Both run on the server and talk to the Admin GraphQL API, version 2026-10, with your shop's access token. And the API reads or changes real products in the store.

Nothing here is mock data. Why GraphQL and not REST? Shopify marked the REST Admin API as legacy in October 2024, and new public apps have to use GraphQL.

And with GraphQL you ask for exactly the fields you need, in one request, instead of whatever an endpoint decides to send. Before any code runs, the app needs permission. In shopify.app.toml, the scope write products covers reading and changing products.

Then one line in the app navigation adds the Products page to the admin sidebar. Here's that page. Ten products, newest first, with status, inventory, price and vendor, all from the API.

Notice the order. The query sorts by updated at, newest first, so anything you create or edit jumps straight to the top. My workflow for every feature in this series: test the query in GraphiQL, then copy it into the app.

If it works in GraphiQL, it works in the app.

Read: query products (2:09)

Let's start with reading products, and I'll show every query in GraphiQL first, so you see exactly what Shopify returns. This is the products query. I ask for five products whose title contains snowboard.

Shopify returns the two snowboards in my store, with their status and lowest price, plus pageInfo for the next page. GraphiQL here comes with shopify app dev: press g in the terminal and it opens with your app's own scopes and your dev store. And look at the IDs.

Every Shopify object has a global ID like gid shopify product and a number. That's what every mutation needs. In the app, the same query lives at the top of the products route.

First or last says how many, after or before are the cursors, and query is the search text. Below that, I list only the fields the table shows. Smaller queries cost less, and Shopify rate limits by cost.

The loader runs this query on the server every time the page opens. It reads the search text and the cursor from the URL, so search and pages are just links. Search uses title with wildcards on both sides, so snow finds snowboard.

And the page receives plain data. Here it is in the app. I type snowboard and press enter.

Two results, the same two GraphiQL gave us. The search box is a Polaris s search field. One honest note: pressing enter inside s search field doesn't submit a normal form, so I listen for the enter key myself.

Pages work the same way. Next page sends the endCursor, and Shopify gives the next ten. Previous page sends the startCursor.

No page numbers: Shopify uses cursors so pages stay stable. The table fires next page and previous page events. React eighteen doesn't bind custom events, so I add the listeners directly.

Create: productCreate (4:09)

Now let's create a product. The add product button opens a Polaris modal. Title, description, status, price, vendor, product type and tags.

Every one of these goes to Shopify. I set the price to twenty four ninety nine. Keep an eye on the price, because there's a trap here.

Watch it in GraphiQL. productCreate with a title, a status and a vendor. The product exists, but look at the variant: price zero.

productCreate doesn't take a price at all. While we're here, scroll down. Every response tells you what it cost.

This mutation cost thirteen points. My app has two thousand points available, and they refill at a hundred per second. Big queries cost more, so ask only for what you show.…

item.title: A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud company IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

Earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a new class of hardware.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a new processor that takes care of the heavy math.

The cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

How would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

Light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

It coincides with Smart Window's first expansion beyond North America and marks a deliberate attempt by Mozilla to resist the pattern of browser makers coupling tightly to a single American AI provider.

Smart Window, originally announced in November 2025 as "AI Window", operates as an optional window separate from regular browsing. It helps users make sense of complex searches, group related tabs, revisit pages they have seen before and carry work across sessions. Users decide when to use it, which model to use and what browsing context to share. Conversations are not stored on Mozilla's servers by default, and Mistral has agreed to zero data retention for the partnership.

Mistral Small 4 is a 119-billion-parameter model distributed on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence. Mozilla selected it after evaluating performance in the beta, with multilingual quality as a central criterion. According to Cybernews, the partnership expands Mistral's reach by approximately 200,000 active monthly Firefox users, giving the French company its first large consumer distribution channel outside its own Le Chat app.

Mozilla Corporation CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo framed the deal as a bet on openness: "A browser shouldn't be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next." Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch described the collaboration as "two open source advocates working together."

The move puts Firefox alongside, but distinct from, Chrome's Gemini integration, Edge's Copilot sidebar and Opera's Aria. In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO.

Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”

But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”

Patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and quickly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals

The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

Fee details

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

'Extraordinary powers'

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

Cracked sea walls held together by tape and plywood, submerged roads blocked by cones and police officers, and businesses with “Closed” signs sheltered behind sand bags decorated the area for Thanksgiving.

The tidal inundation during the holiday week—excacerbated by the “Kelvin Wave,” a pulse of warm water making its way up the West Coast—offered a preview of what may be in store for Christmas, and longer term, thanks to the current El Niño.

In Northern California, Pacifica, a city southwest of San Francisco, lost part of its pier to savage ocean waves. To the south, San Diego issued boardwalk closures amid surging water levels.

The king tides peaked on Wednesday, bringing record high water to parts of Southern California. In Los Angeles, the tide peaked at 8.19 feet above the average low tide, tying the record set just last month. Further down the coast, in La Jolla, waves smashed into houses, also breaking the high tide record just a month after it had been set. King tides, the highest astronomical tides of the year, occur during the winter months when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon are at their peak.

Ahead of the Thanksgiving Day flooding, climatologist Daniel Swain noted that the overlap between water levels consistently running above usual levels was not due to the storms. They were happening because of the overlap between the king tides and the climate-amplified super El Niño, he said.

Joseph Lucey-Renteria, an assistant professor in the Civil Engineering Department at California State University, Los Angeles, said “it’s supposed to be worse in December, and then we’re supposed to have some similar levels that we’re seeing today, but now in January.”

Lucey-Renteria was joined by students in Sunset Beach to capture footage of the flooding as part of a project aimed at modeling for inclement weather and preparing for future storms and tides.

“They were lucky that the waves weren’t very very large today or that there wasn’t a rain event coming in,” Lucey-Renteria said.

Throughout Naples, an affluent enclave in Long Beach, residents saw their canals fill to the brim due to the rising tide—threatening multi-million-dollar homes.

In 2024, Long Beach put a $125 million project to retrofit the area’s aging sea walls on hold briefly when the price tag of the first two phases ballooned. An anticipated steep decline in the area’s oil production left the “Tidelands Operations Fund” with a severe budget deficit, according to local officials.

The project has since resumed but is progressing slowly, homeowners said, leaving the 90-year-old, heavily eroded sea walls further deteriorating, with every tidal swing, to contend with the historic flooding.

Local high school principal Erik Nielson, 59, teamed up with neighbor Eric Mears to temporarily add about two feet of height to sea walls in Naples with sheets of plywood. That was braced to a foundering wall near canal-side homes with duct tape and spray foam insulation.

Mears, 62, who grew up in Naples and has lived there most of his life, spent Tuesday morning checking how the makeshift repairs to the 90-year-old sea wall were holding up. Overall, the software engineer was impressed with how the neighbors’ DIY solutions had reduced the flooding, compared to what occurred during the October spring tides.

On the other side of Naples Island, Michelle Shea, a block captain and attorney, felt responsible for how her neighbors fared during the inundation and was worried about the future of the island.

Shea, who grew up in Naples and whose grandfather built the home she lives in, recently turned her attention to the infrastructure protecting her neighborhood from the ocean—dirt-filled sand bags.

“We have water leaking from places we’ve never seen before,” Shea said, while looking at her own sea wall.

Water was pumped away near Mitry’s Sunset Beach home, which did not have extensive damage during this week’s high tides. However, her neighbor, Jerry Cimmarusti, was standing in a pool of water in front of his home on Thanksgiving Day.

The first floor of an apartment Cimmarusti, 72, rents out a few blocks away became uninhabitable after it was inundated during an October storm. He wasn’t taking any chances this week.

Cimmarusti and his family set up close to 300 sand bags to prepare for the flood. Now, he needs local officials to cut part of the storm grate in front of his home in order to pump water out. If they don’t do that in time for December high tides, his son, Charlie, joked, “He’s gonna take matters into his own hands.”

About 12 miles to the south, Craig Auger, the utility supervisor who oversees stormwater operations for Newport Beach, called in more manpower, from about 20 staff members to roughly 60, given the tide projections. Why it is here: Detailed reporting on illegal wildlife trade with useful context.

From lizards to snakes, Hong Kong is emerging as a primary trafficking center for native Australian reptiles, reports contributor Selina Cheng for Mongabay.

In December 2025, customs authorities intercepted a consignment from Australia containing 13 live lizards stuffed inside winter boots. Hong Kong’s customs agency said the air cargo was falsely declared as snacks.

This was the fourth such seizure of live native Australian reptiles by Hong Kong customs authorities between 2025 and 2026. Across the four seizures, officials confiscated at least 98 animals, including 74 lizards and 24 snakes, valued at more than HK$1.1 million ($141,100).

Intelligence briefing papers from researchers at the Wildlife Crime Research Hub at Adelaide University in Australia confirmed that Hong Kong “functions both as a destination and a potential transit hub within broader trafficking networks.”

In Australia, keeping native reptiles as pets is strictly regulated and requires a license. But Hong Kong and mainland China don’t require proof of legal origin or documentation for possession. This has allowed illegally smuggled wildlife to be “laundered” in Hong Kong’s legal trade.

Australia has since 1982 also banned commercial exports of live native species. However, an estimated 15% of Australia’s endemic reptile species have entered illicit international trade, according to the Wildlife Crime Research Hub.

Dylan Chadwick, from the research hub, told Mongabay that demand is high for skinks in the genus Tiliqua, including the shingleback (Tiliqua rugosa), nicknamed the “pine cone lizard” in China.

“Reptiles gained immense popularity during Covid lockdowns as low-maintenance pets, with buyers drawn to unique color morphs and exotic features — almost like collecting Pokémon,” Chadwick said.

Charlie Zhu, a reptile seller based in Changzhou, a city in eastern China, told Mongabay that there’s a growing market for breeding Australian reptiles in the country. But desirable species like shinglebacks are difficult to breed in captivity, driving market prices that start at around 20,000 Chinese yuan ($3,000).

According to the ADM Capital Foundation (ADMCF), a Hong Kong-based environmental nonprofit that tracks wildlife crime, Hong Kong authorities made nearly 5,000 seizures of endangered species between 2015 and 2025, worth nearly HK$1.2 billion ($153,000). The organization also warned that smuggling operations in Hong Kong have attracted organized crime syndicates. The Australian government said these syndicates are increasingly recruiting international students to transport animals out of the country. One student from China was sentenced to 18 months in jail last year on wildlife trafficking charges.

Hong Kong added wildlife trafficking to its Organized and Serious Crimes Ordinance in 2021. However, Sam Inglis of ADMCF said penalties imposed by courts remain far below the maximum legal limits.

“What is missing is the systematic dismantling of these networks,” Inglis said. “Smugglers consider a one-year prison sentence just a cost of doing business.”

Why it is here: In-depth look at elephant conservation efforts with expert opinions.

A beloved male elephant named Kavantissa that frequented a rural village in Sri Lanka recently died from a gunshot injury, sparking public outrage. Environmentalists condemned authorities for what they called a “lack of care” for this iconic elephant, while local animal rights groups demanded an independent investigation into the death.

In response, the Sri Lankan government launched a military operation called Hasthi Sena, which translates to an “elephant army,” reports contributor Malaka Rodrigo for Mongabay.

This task force brings together some 100 members from Sri Lanka’s armed forces and departments of wildlife and civil defense. Its goal is to prevent further elephant killings, curb wildlife crime, and bolster surveillance across hotspots of human-elephant encounters. As of early November, the task force had already arrested individuals involved in illegal activities such as setting wire snares and using trap guns.

Since Kavantissa’s death, public support for assigning armed personnel to elephants with large tusks. Such tuskers, as they’re known are rare among Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). In Sri Lanka, a 1999 study estimated that only about 7.5% of male elephants are tuskers.

Over the past 10 years, advocacy group Wild Tuskers Srilanka (WTS) has documented 300 such elephants. The group also recently identified 17 tuskers as being at high risk and needing urgent monitoring, in part due to the overlap of their ranges with human settlements, said Chandika Lakshan, a WTS member. The organization has handed over the detailed profiles of the 17 tuskers to government and military officials.

However, wildlife experts have cautioned against military intervention to protect elephants. Manori Gunawardena, a wildlife scientist at the Environmental Foundation Limited, said that unlike African super tuskers living in vast protected reserves, Sri Lanka’s elephants roam densely inhabited agricultural landscapes where direct physical guarding is impractical. She added that ivory poaching in the country is largely a byproduct of broader human-elephant conflict rather than of organized international syndicates.

“We must meet the ecological needs of the herds that produce tuskers, ensuring that male calves and juveniles survive into adulthood if we are truly committed to the future of Sri Lanka’s wild tuskers,” Gunawardena told Mongabay. “This requires sufficient and suitable habitats and socially inclusive, scientifically informed measures to reduce human-elephant conflict.”

Hemantha Withanage, senior adviser to the Centre for Environmental Justice (CEJ), said law enforcement should focus on intelligence gathering rather than posting a soldier beside every identified tusker. He cited the persistent use of “jaw bombs” by some poachers, who scatter balls of food bait packed with explosives to kill wild boars and other animals for meat. Elephants that fall victim to these bait balls suffer gruesome injuries and long-drawn-out deaths. Withanage said military intelligence is well-suited to dismantling the illicit supply of the explosives used in these jaw bombs.

item.title: In Nepal, experts debate future of mega-dams after August’s flood
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion on the impact of mega-dams with contrasting viewpoints.

- On Aug. 26, a catastrophic flood killed more than 1,353 and has reopened Nepal’s debate over mega-dams.

- Proponents say high reservoir dams could absorb floods and ease winter power shortages.

- Those against such dams say stored water adds risk if a glacial lake bursts, and support solar and pumped storage as alternatives.

- Research suggests Himalayan hydropower is widely exposed to such floods but, so far, no study has tested whether reservoirs worsen them.

KATHMANDU — Until recently, residents living in the lap of the Himalayas saw the peaks as immovable giants silently nurturing them with snowmelt.

But on Aug. 26, there was a road from the mountain overlooking the Bhotekoshi rivershed in central Nepal roared. What appears to have been an avalanche on Langtang Lirung sent a churning wall of water, mud and boulders down the valley. In Nepal, more than 1,353 people were killed and many thousands went missing. The flood also damaged at least a dozen hydropower projects.

As the flood receded, a debate surfaced in Nepal’s policy circles about the future of hydropower. Some experts now advocate mega-dams in the Himalayas to contain large floods, manage winter power shortages and even prepare for a future without snow in the Himalaya. But limits to engineering and earthquakes in the young mountains challenge any such endeavor, experts tell Mongabay.

“The question for the future is not whether Nepal will continue to develop its rivers,” writes David Fickling, climate and energy columnist for Bloomberg. “It is whether the next generation of hydro projects merely extracts electricity with run-of-river, or builds storage dams to give downstream communities greater protection against the consequences of our increasingly deadly climate.”

Reservoir dams, which store large volumes of water and generate electricity on demand, have long been part of government policy. The pro-dam camp points to Kulekhani, located southwest of Kathmandu, which generates 92 GWh (Gigawatt-hour) annually and helps meet winter peak demand. But the four-decade-old plant is the only one of its kind in the country. All other operating plants are run-of-river, which divert flowing water without storing it, so their output drops to less than half of installed capacity in the dry season.

Privately operated generators, who supply nearly 60% of the country’s electricity, have been reluctant to build reservoirs because of the steep costs and risks, says Mohan Kumar Dangi, chair of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN).

The case for mega-dams

Geologist Bishal Nath Upreti, who taught geology at Kathmandu’s Tribhuvan University for 35 years, says he believes high dams can hold the water and debris of mega flash floods and give downstream communities time to evacuate. “High dams are safe if geological studies are properly conducted and designed with the latest technology,” he tells Mongabay.

Dangi from IPPAN says high dams are also needed to address winter power shortages. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) expects domestic plants to generate 1,218 MW this winter, against peak demand of 2,250 to 2,300 MW. It reportedly plans to import 1,154 MW from India — roughly half of what the country needs at peak.

Hitendra Dev Shakya, former managing director of the NEA, says reservoirs could also protect water supplies as mountain snow disappears. An ICIMOD report suggests that under current emissions pathways 80% of glaciers’ current volume will be gone by 2100. A decline is already visible: ICIMOD’s latest snow update in April found that snow persistence, the proportion of time that snow is on the ground in a given period, in the Hindu Kush Himalaya was 27.8% below average in 2026, the lowest level in 24 years.

There’s limited knowledge on what this could potentially mean for hydropower generated from perennial snow-fed rivers. Preliminary modeling of four major basins, presented at a conference in 2024 and not yet peer reviewed, found generation potential could rise by up to 36% by 2100 as meltwater increases. Drier scenarios pointed towards the .

Shakya told Mongabay dams should serve multiple purposes, including providing drinking water, flood control and irrigation, and the cost of construction as well as operation should not fall on electricity users alone.

Storage dams in the pipeline

The Tanahu Seti dam, in Seti River in Gandaki province, with storage of 300 million cubic meters (around 79 billion gallons), is scheduled to start operating next year. At least two others are ready for construction, including the 263-meter (863-feet) Budhigandaki, which would store 4.467 million m3 (around 1.2 billion gal). West Seti, Pancheshwor and Saptakoshi High Dam are at earlier stages.

Budhigandaki is estimated to cost around $2.77 billion. In his budget speech for the current fiscal year in May, Finance Minister Swarnim Waglé announced plans to build it through a special purpose vehicle using the country’s own resources. The government has spent more than 45 billion Nepalese rupees (around $301 million) on land acquisition and has listed it as a “priority project” for over a decade.

Case against mega-dams

Opponents argue that stored water adds risk in the event of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), when a lake high in the mountains suddenly bursts.

Dwarika Nath Dhungel, a water resources expert and former government secretary, says the Bhotekoshi flood has reinforced his anti-dam stance. “We feel like ‘living just below an atom bomb of the glacial lakes’ which may fall upon us at any time,” he tells Mongabay. “So much information is out there on dams and it’s high time to change our way of thinking of the dams.”…

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of community forestry initiatives with challenges and opportunities.

- As an initiative aimed at securing land rights, strengthening community governance, and preserving forests, community forestry is gaining significant ground in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where it’s generating genuine interest among communities.

- However, at the local level, the implementation of measures designed to regulate its management faces several challenges, as two experts point out in an interview with Mongabay.

- In particular, Blaise Mudodosi and Védaste Cituli highlight the obstacles to the profitability of these conservation initiatives; the lack of synergy among public services; and the lack of coordination in community forestry processes.

- Communities that have prospered and are now beginning to generate significant income are those that are developing activities related to cacao and coffee cultivation, particularly on fallow land, as well as sustainable fishing.

LUBUMBASHI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an initiative is underway to award community-based forestry land titles to 7.1 million hectares of land, or about 17.5 million acres — an area the size of Ireland. This is one of several conservation strategies aimed at protecting the DRC’s biodiversity while recognizing customary rights over the land.

Apart from the protected areas that have been formally established to date and the vast Kivu-Kinshasa green corridor, the number of local community forest concessions (CFCLs) has risen from eight in 2017 to more than 350 in 2026, of which at least 236 have been legally established.

However, while they provide the legal framework that protects communities from unjust or arbitrary expropriation, and allow certain communities to benefit from their forests, CFCLs also have the task of creating opportunities for communities. Without these opportunities, some communities are tempted to illegally exploit their own forests.

One decade after the ministerial decree that established the rules for managing and operating these concessions, Mongabay’s Didier Makal speaks with two experts in the sector to get their take on progress.

Blaise Mudodosi, a doctoral researcher at the University of Goma in the DRC, works on the implementation and evaluation of community forestry projects and serves as the national coordinator of the NGO Actions for the Promotion and Protection of Threatened Peoples and Species (APEM), an environmental organization founded in 2013. His work and observations focus in particular on the security and governance of CFCL, as well as the economic utilization of forest resources and institutional support mechanisms.

Védaste Cituli, who holds a Ph.D. focused in particular on CFCLs in South Kivu province, in the eastern DRC, is a researcher at the Higher Institute for Rural Development in Bukavu (ISDR-Bukavu), where he examines power dynamics within communities, the participation of women and Indigenous peoples in forest management bodies, and issues related to securing land rights and preserving Indigenous knowledge.

Mudodosi and Cituli point to, among other challenges and obstacles to the profitability of these conservation projects, a lack of synergy between government agencies and a lack of coordination in community forestry processes. They also discuss of solutions to help community forestry projects generate profits and continue to engage local communities.

The following interview has been translated from French and lightly edited for length and style.

Mongabay: How would you assess community forestry in the DRC after about 10 years of implementation?

Blaise Mudodosi: This is a process in which the communities have placed a great deal of hope. Some results are beginning to show, particularly in terms of areas that have already been secured. That’s the most important part. But when it comes to the management, use, and production of resources, things are still moving a bit slowly.

On the other hand, there are many constraints, particularly regarding the communities’ financial and technical capabilities. But for the communities, the fact that they already have a concession provides a sense of security.

Védaste Cituli: The community forest approach is to be applauded. It is truly a vital initiative for forest conservation, but also for the preservation of Indigenous knowledge that contributes to their conservation.

Unfortunately, at the local level, implementing the measures that have been put in place poses a problem. [Sometimes,] communities have been forced to pay large sums of money [to officials and government agencies], contrary to the law, which stipulates that the permit should be issued free of charge. As a result, corruption is taking root throughout the entire process of obtaining the permit.

It should also be noted that in some societies, women are still disadvantaged. They face difficulties gaining access to forest management or governance committees established at the local level. The same is true for Indigenous peoples. Since they are a minority, they continue to face discrimination and have difficulty accessing decision-making positions in forest management committees.

Let me give an example: When management committees are formed, voting is done by a show of hands. Yet we thought this approach should include all social strata as much as possible.

Mongabay: What are the main obstacles to communities’ economic use of forest resources? In other words, their capacity to sustainably use the resources as a basis of their livelihoods.

Védaste Cituli: Local communities don’t really always have the knowledge needed to manage these community forests.

There is also the issue of support. After obtaining the governor’s decree [establishing a CFCL], the NGOs [supporting communities in this process] are often limited in their capacity and rarely assist communities all the way through the development of basic management plans.…

Why it is here: one short sentence

“We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism” says curator of Geoffrey Bawa exhibition at Vitra Design Museum

As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the ‘tropical modernist’ label has confused Bawa’s legacy.

Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia’s most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.

Bawa’s work is often described as tropical modernist, as it is seen to blend Western modernist principles with Sri Lankan vernacular traditions and materials.

But Deurell said he and his co-curators deliberately stayed away from this label, which was coined by Western architects and scholars and is closely associated with British colonialism.

“We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism,” he told Dezeen.

“It comes with so much baggage. But it’s also not the most useful tool to discuss Geoffrey Bawa’s work with.”

As one of the Vitra Design Museum’s in-house curators, Deurell oversaw the show with Shayari de Silva, chief curator for the Geoffrey Bawa Trust, and Ikko Yokoyama, a senior curator at M+ in Hong Kong.

The exhibition offers a broader understanding of Bawa’s legacy, highlighting qualities that set him apart from the modernists.

For instance, it highlights how his buildings worked with existing landscape conditions.

“He built with nature rather than against it,” Deurell said.

“Modernist site planning often involved clearing the land, rather than having buildings like Kandalama Hotel, which snakes its way around a rift.”

The show also spotlights the sustainability of Bawa’s designs, in terms of both ecology and socioeconomics.

His buildings harnessed the skills of local craftspeople and were built with locally sourced materials. They also featured climate-conscious strategies for shading and ventilation.

This approach is particularly relevant today, said Deurell, as the building industry faces the reality of a climate crisis.

“His ideas on landscape and ecology was really at the forefront,” the curator said. “He had a holistic approach to architecture and he built with nature in mind.”

The exhibition features a scenography designed by Lina Ghotmeh, who was named Dezeen Awards’ Architect of the Year 2026. It contains over 250 exhibits, including drawings, models, archive photography and furniture.

Among the highlights is a new photography series by Iwan Baan, capturing 11 of Bawa’s buildings as never seen before.

Drone photography offers a look at Bawa’s Number 11 house and University of Ruhuna from above, while other shots show people occupying the Lighthouse Hotel and Bentota Beach Hotel.

Furniture on show includes a mix of original Bawa designs and versions of well-known modernist pieces remade with local materials.

As Deurell explains, these were not intended as copies. The originals were not available in Sri Lanka at that time, so Bawa simply commissioned replicas for use in his interiors.

Standouts include a version of the Barcelona Chair by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, with a welded iron frame and stripy upholstery fabric designed by Sri Lankan designer Barbara Sansoni.

“Bawa collaborated with artists throughout his career, ” said Deurell, pointing to long-standing collaborations with Ena de Silva and Laki Senanayake as well as Sansoni.

“All of these artists ran their practices as social enterprises, so they would employ villagers and train them in a craft,” stated the curator. “It shows the social consciousness within his practice.”

Drawings bring another dimension to the exhibition. Highly detailed maps, floor plans and sectional drawings emphasise the relationship between building and landscape.

Although these drawings were mostly produced after the buildings were completed, they offer an insight into the architect’s mindset.

Deurell points to a quote by Bawa, where he talks about landscape elements as being part of “the total picture”.

“They are just as important as the architecture itself”, he said.

Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader

“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H.P. Lovecraft advised aspiring writers. We’ve already seen that reading is a learned skill and an optimizable technique, and that non-reading is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a good reader?

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life. He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected Lectures on Literature (public library), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:

- The reader should belong to a book club.

- The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.

- The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.

- The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.

- The reader should have seen the book in a movie.

- The reader should be a budding author.

- The reader should have imagination.

- The reader should have memory.

- The reader should have a dictionary.

- The reader should have some artistic sense.

The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Complement with Mark Twain’s humorous list of the fourteen types of readers and Nabokov on the three qualities a great storyteller must have.

The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on why we fall and how we stay in love. “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist Donald Hall (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of Poetry — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in “the bead of sensation” that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do?”

What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.

What we did: love.

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing Little Prince author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s beautiful insistence that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.

For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach on Eagle Pond. Soft moss underfoot sent little red flowers up. Ghost birches leaned over water with wild strawberry plants growing under them. Over our heads white pines reared high, and oaks that warned us of summer’s end late in August by dropping green metallic acorns. Sometimes a mink scooted among ferns… Jane dozed in the sun as I sat in the shade reading and occasionally taking a note in a blank book. From time to time we swam and dried in the heat.

Hall’s most piercing point is that the third thing, rather than being an extraneous adornment of the relationship, is a central form of companionship. But while it is indispensable, it is not irreplaceable — it doesn’t so much matter what the thing is, only that it is.

When a landfill leakage destroyed their beloved pond, Hall and Kenyon still had their other third thing — poetry. Reflecting on its unparalleled power of perspective, its power to connect and console in the face of life’s darkest moments, he writes:

We lived in the house of poetry, which was also the house of love and grief; the house of solitude and art; the house of Jane’s depression and my cancers and Jane’s leukemia. When someone died whom we loved, we went back to the poets of grief and outrage, as far back as Gilgamesh;…

item.description:

Why it is here: explains an idea clearly, useful vocabulary

One of the most counterintuitive things about existence is the notion of forces. In order to experience a force — that is, for one object to feel the influence of another object on it — two objects don’t necessarily even need to touch, or be in contact, with one another. Objects on Earth’s surface feel Earth’s gravity, but so do airplanes, satellites, and even the Moon: in the atmosphere, in low-Earth orbit, or even hundreds of thousands of kilometers away. An electrically charged object attracts and repels other electrical charges, regardless of how far away they are from each other. And, in a more familiar fashion, two magnets flipped so that their north poles face each other mutually repel one another so strongly that, for some magnets, even the strongest humans cannot bring them together into contact.

So what happens, then, when you try to bring your thumb and forefinger together? How close do they actually get, and do they ever truly “touch” one another? That’s what Peter Mead wants to know, writing in to ask:

“When I hold both hands out in front of me with my two forefingers pointed toward each other then bring them together, the space between my fingers gets smaller and smaller. I can see and hold them a bit less than a millimeter apart before they touch. Is there an instant, just before they touch, where my fingers are only an atom’s (or sub-atomic) width apart? Or does space somehow behave differently on such a small scale?”

Clearly, there’s a big range in between what we can see (a little under a millimeter) and the size of an atom (about one ten-billionth of a meter). Let’s find out what happens on those tiny scales.

Although we’re going to go down to very small scales to address this question in full, it’s important to recognize that “small” doesn’t necessarily mean “quantum” the way you might intuit. Yes, quantum effects typically rear their heads in isolated, single-or-few particle systems and tend to disappear if there are many particles interacting frequently, which is a hallmark of (most) macroscopic phenomena. However, while quantum effects normally appear on atomic scales or below, the more classical effects — including gravitational and electromagnetic effects — can never be ignored, and frequently dominate even over inherently quantum ones, even on the smallest scales of all.

Therefore, the first step is to recognize that your body is made of atoms, and that while the atoms within your fingers are bound together into molecules that comprise the organelles that make up your cells, it’s still fundamentally all atoms: electrons orbiting atomic nuclei. Even though it’s a long way down from the macroscopic world (fingers) to the atoms and the subatomic particles that make even the atoms up, that’s what the structure of matter truly looks like.

The atoms that are bound together — into molecules and then into larger structures — have restrictions on how their electrons can move. Even when shared between multiple atoms, the electrons orbit in cloud-like shells, and have a smeared-out distribution over time, dependent on what specific energy level (and molecular/atomic orbitals) they occupy. Whether you’re looking at a single atom or a larger structure made out of atoms, that’s the basic picture: there’s a negatively-charged electron cloud orbiting around a single or a series of multiple positively-charged atomic nucleus/nuclei.

Grateful for curious minds

So what happens, then, when you bring two atoms close to one another, as you might imagine happens when you bring your thumb and forefinger close to one another, but not so close as to have them touch?

It’s an interesting problem that most physics students learn how to solve in graduate school, where we all get the same answers if we perform our calculations correctly: the shape of the electron cloud that orbits around the atomic nucleus changes in response to the presence of the other nearby atom. Even though atoms (and molecules) themselves are neutral entities, the fact that they’re made of negatively and positively charged components allows them to do something extremely important: to polarize.

Polarization is a classical electromagnetic phenomenon, occurring wherever you have positive and negative charged together and the ability to have these charges move around and redistribute themselves relative to one another, dependent on the external forces acting on them. It turns out that while having a positive or negative charge nearby is an easy “external force” to visualize, simply bringing two uncharged but polarizable objects close to each other can, in fact, result in not only both objects polarizing, but in a net force being created between the two.

For example, let’s think about two simple atoms that are brought near to one another. Each one has a positively charged atomic nucleus and a diffuse cloud of negative charge around it. If you bring one into the vicinity of the other, they’ll initially remain spherical: with no net attractive or repulsive force. However, the closer you bring them together, the more the electron clouds will distort in their shape, creating a tiny dipole: where one positively charged nucleus is slightly off-center relative to the negatively-charged spherical distribution of the negative charges.…

November 25 sees the release of Focker-In-Law, the newest film in the Meet the Parents franchise. The 2000 installment follows Ben Stiller and his fiancÃ©e, Teri Polo, as he meets her mother and father (played by Blythe Danner and Robert De Niro) for the first time, and the comedic chaos that follows.

However, this movie was not actually an original production: it was a remake of the 1992 indie film of the same title, directed by the filmmaker Greg Glienna. The original is also a much darker film than its more famous remake: as Variety put it, "Who ever heard of a comedy where everyone gets maimed, drowned, shot or commits suicide?... 'Meet the Parents' turns a visit with the in-laws into a living nightmare." Here's a look at the original film on which a long-running franchise was built (and which the distributor later tried to keep the public from seeing).

Inside the Indie That Inspired Meet the Parents

Like the later version of the story, the 1992 film explores the idea of what happens when a man meets his future in-laws, but in Glienna's version, it ventures into much more serious territory, with multiple characters being killed as the story unfolds. Unlike the expensive Hollywood remake, the original was shot on a budget of only $30,000, and in addition to directing, Glienna played the lead role and co-wrote the script with Mary Ruth Clark. The project was originally sold to National Lampoon to be released as part of their self-titled series of films, but the deal fell through, leaving its future uncertain at first. Â

However, it received some positive critical attention when it made its debut: Variety reviewed the film when it premiered at the 1992 Just for Laughs Comedy Festival in Montreal, and described it as a "wonderfully twisted dark comedy." Their review also gives a number of details about the little-seen movie's story, including their summary of the plot's framing device: "Presented almost entirely in flashback, the tale begins when a gas station attendant warns a client en route to meet the future in-laws to 'turn back' while he still can. What follows is the tragic story of a previous future groom who didnât take the advice." The disasters which befall the characters include a saga in which "Greg blinds the mother with a fishing rod, ruins the family car, drowns the dog and accidentally climbs into bed with his fiancÃ©e's sister."

How a Tricky Contract Locked It Away

The original film was not widely distributed, but according to Glienna, one person who did see it was Steven Soderbergh, who liked it so much that he reached out to the writer-director about developing the original into a new version: "He called me and said this should be a big studio film â this is very commercial. And they flew my co-writer, Mary Ruth Clark and myself to New York to work with him for three days, and we worked on the script â his vision of it." Ultimately, Universal acquired the rights to the film with the intention to make a new version based on the same premise.

However, after Glienna sold the remake rights to Universal, it turned out there was a catch in his deal. In a 2024 interview, Glienna explained: "I got a lousy lawyer, and we signed a contract. I don't know why this wasn't explained to me, or I didn't comprehend it, but I could only release it after a certain amount of time in a not-for-profit situation. I don't know why I would have agreed to that. Now, anytime I've tried to get the rights to release the film, they say no. I don't know why they don't want me to release this film."

Glienna expressed his disappointment at the hurdle which had been placed in front of his original version. "We made this film to be seen. Why would they not let us show [it to] people? I don't understand." However, Glienna has attempted to look for the positives in the situation: "I try to look on the bright side. â¦ I'm still getting residuals on something I did 30 years ago." Today, the original film occasionally emerges on YouTube, but it remains to be seen whether it will ever be officially cleared for re-release in the future.

item.description:

What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players -have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

Rummenigge goes on the offensive

A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

Bayern under pressure during contract negotiations

Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, Â£21m a year, with Â£15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to Â£25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.…

item.title: How Fury and Joshua changed British boxing forever
