How Fury and Joshua changed British boxing forever

They have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.

Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.

They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.

Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.

Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.

We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.

Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.

How Fury and Joshua brought big-time heavyweight boxing to Britain

Britain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas.

Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.

In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight.

"Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.

Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard.

"I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.

By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA.

"The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."

Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.

Crossover stars who inspired the next crop of heavyweights

Fury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.

Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night.

"You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for Â£2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.

Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.

Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.

Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.

Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."

Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.

Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".

The final question of their legacy

Yet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?

After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".

For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.

In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.

Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place.

"Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says.

But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved.

"Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.

The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff.

But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.

Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs

- Published

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations rules between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

- Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

- Published19 November

- Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

- Published6 October

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by Â£900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

item.title: Writing Is Not a Checkpoint: Teaching Contextual Judgment in the AI Era
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

At the public library desk, questions about writing often arrive as requests for technical help. Patrons drafting personal statements need to decide which details about their experience to include; people completing online forms need to interpret questions before answering them. Helping patrons make writing decisions has been as much a part of my library work as explaining where to click.

I encounter similar questions in online writing courses. Students bring rules such as “never use I,” “always write five paragraphs,” and “never use artificial intelligence.” Some rules are assignment requirements; others are writing conventions students have learned to apply everywhere. Contextual judgment requires understanding what a rule accomplishes and when it applies. Students need opportunities to explain their choices within course requirements and ask for clarification when an expectation is unclear.

Rhetoric and composition scholar Sharon Crowley described required freshman English as a “border checkpoint,” where students had to establish their right to belong in higher education (1991, 160). She argued for ending the universal requirement while retaining the course as an elective (170). I draw on her account of gatekeeping to ask a narrower classroom question: How can instructors teach judgment while assessing compliance with assignment requirements? AI policies establish what is permitted; instruction must help students judge whether a permitted use serves the assignment’s purpose. The following examples illustrate ways to teach contextual judgment through activities and feedback you can adapt to your own courses.

Start with the Rules Students Bring

Nancy Walker, who helped me learn to teach writing, was an English professor and director of freshman English at what was then Southwest Missouri State University. In her 1987 statement, “Thoughts About Teaching,” she described how students could move from rigid right-or-wrong thinking to the belief that every judgment was a matter of personal preference. She called for “contextual deciding,” in which students evaluate ideas in context, commit to a choice, and remain willing to reconsider it (2).

A writing rules inventory offers one way to practice contextual deciding. Early in the course, ask students to list three rules they have learned. Have them choose one and explain where they learned it, what purpose it might serve, and when it might be useful. Follow the inventory with examples that test the rule’s limits.

To test “never use I,” compare two sentences. “I interviewed three residents” identifies who gathered the evidence. If a writer has verified a survey’s respondent count, adding “I believe” to “The survey had 40 respondents” makes the count sound uncertain. In this example, the qualification is unnecessary; the first-person pronoun is not the problem. Ask students to explain the difference, revise the rule, and test it on a sentence from a draft. Discuss how the revised rule accounts for the writer’s purpose.

Make Transfer Explicit

Walker urged teachers to plan activities that make discovery possible (1987, 1–2). Students who have already written a research paper may need help identifying what a new research task asks them to do differently.

The Elon Statement on Writing Transfer emphasizes reflection on how writers adapt prior learning to new tasks (Center for Engaged Learning 2015). For a memo recommending a course of action to a busy supervisor, ask students to write a brief transfer note before they draft the memo. Which practices from an earlier research essay can they reuse? What will they need to change for this reader and purpose?

Ask students to identify one adjustment, such as placing a recommendation before its supporting explanation. After students draft the memo, have them revisit the note and explain how a specific passage addresses the supervisor’s needs. Compare the passage with the explanation and give feedback on any needed revision. Students can consult the note when deciding whether the same strategy fits a later assignment.

Use the Problem as Material

Walker described a student who was stuck writing about his father. She helped him notice that his draft expressed affection as well as criticism (1987, 3–4). When students hesitate over an AI revision, ask them to compare the original and suggested wording and explain how the change affects the claim. The Association for Writing Across the Curriculum recommends reflection on whether and how AI serves a writing task (AWAC Working Group on AI in WAC 2025).

Explain permitted uses of AI before students begin an assignment. A process note does not authorize prohibited assistance. After major assignments in my online writing courses, I ask for an AI Use Note or process note that acknowledges assistance and examines the writer’s decisions:

- What tools or other assistance did you use, and for which parts of the assignment?

- Which suggestions did you accept, change, or reject, and why?

- How did you check the claims and sources you used?

- What alternatives did you consider for one writing decision, and why did you choose your approach?

Students who worked without AI can describe research and revision decisions. For students who used AI, the note should address how they evaluated AI suggestions and whether their use met the assignment’s rules. Instructors can collect the note with a draft and give feedback students can use during revision.

If students cite a source without reading it, ask them to read it and check whether it supports the claim. Have students correct any unsupported claim or inaccurate citation. Read the note alongside the draft to discuss whether the explanation matches the writing. A plausible explanation alone does not establish authorship or compliance.…

item.title: Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear structure, useful vocabulary

It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. How will your class help them meet their career goals and improve their job skills? Addressing those questions in course planning and design can yield impressive results including increased focus and motivation, a positive effect on students’ approach to assignments, and changing viewpoints on homework assignments as valuable learning experiences.

These outcomes can be achieved with three simple steps: a first day discussion, homework that asks students to read about classroom skills in action and reflect on how they will use the same skills in their careers, and TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) assignments that show students the purpose for homework and/or major assignments.

1. The First Day Discussion

Instead of starting class with introductions or discussing the syllabus, start by asking students how they think your class will help them. In my freshman English classes I ask, “Why do you think NSU requires this class? Why do you think it might be important?” Prompt them to brainstorm why the class is part of their degree program. What skills will they learn that will help them in other classes, their lives, and careers? Write the answers on the board or type them and project them onto a screen. Put added emphasis on career skills learned and give examples of how they will be used.

For example, in my English course I might mention using narrative writing skills when preparing an accident report for a police officer or a client progress report for a physical therapist or using argument essay skills to write a proposal for new equipment at work.

2. Homework About Skills In Action

Use interviews or case studies of the skills in action in the workplace for each unit. In my English 1010 course I have students read an interview with a working professional discussing narrative writing, evaluations, and argument essay skills and how they use them on the job. Once students read the interviews, I ask them to write one or two paragraphs discussing how they will use this skill or skills in their daily lives, in classes, and/or in their future careers.

Good interviews are provided in The McGraw Hill Guide, 5th edition and Business Communication Today, 16th edition. Interviews are also available online or a guest speaker could be invited to the class.

If you only have time to make one change, this one generated the most positive feedback on student surveys.

3. TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) Assignments

TILTed assignments are constructed around a Purpose, Task, and Criteria. I reworked each major assignment in my freshman English classes to meet the TILTed framework for Spring 2026, focusing especially on the purpose section. This strongly connects the writing task with the reasons for doing it such as meeting objectives of the class and future workforce duties.

For example, for a narrative writing assignment, the purpose was as follows: “This assignment eases you into the types of academic writing expected in a college setting while also letting you express yourself creatively by writing your own story. It helps you meet the goals and objectives of the class by demonstrating writing as a purpose-driven process of communication and demonstrating writing to diverse audiences, for a specific purpose, in a specific context. It also enhances skills needed for the workplace where narrative is part of many different writing tasks such as writing an incident report for a police officer, writing a patient progress report for a physical therapist, or writing a pupil progress report as a teacher.

More information about TILTed assignments is available at https://www.tilthighered.com/resources or https://www.uwidocs.org/2020/03/31/tilt-your-assignment-prompts/.

Results—What Did Students Think?

Throughout the Spring 2026 semester, through talking to students and grading homework submissions, I knew the new framework was helpful, but I also gathered data for the TILTed versus unTILTed assignments in my online literature course and the overall framework using all three moves in my freshman English courses. Students were given a Microsoft Forms survey to complete with extra credit points given for participation.

When rating the workforce skills homework assignments where they read an interview with a working professional discussing using the learned skills and then reflected on how they would use them in their own lives, 81% of the students said the homework helped them see the essays “as a valuable learning experience rather than just ‘busy’ work.”

Further, 95% of students said the homework assignments helped them to understand the relevance of each essay type for their future careers.

Ranking from 1 to 5, with 5 being the highest level, students ranked reflecting on the practical applications of these essay types as affecting their focus and motivation while writing the essays at a 4.24 level overall. Since focus and motivation are often lacking in English courses, I was happy to see such positive results in this area.

Students were also asked “if the homework assignments about workplace skills helped you improve focus and motivation when writing the essays, explain how and why.”

Among the more positive comments were, “[It] helped me see a point to the writing,” “It allowed me to put in perspective how important it is to learn how to write correctly and how I will use this in my future career,” and “When doing these homeworks they were not just busy work they were a way to help reflect on what we would be doing and how we should go about writing these essays in an appropriate way.”…

item.description:

Why it is here: In-depth analysis, clear prose, and historical context provide valuable learning and insight.

Immigration stats are down but will that be the end of the issue?

Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration over the last couple of decades.

There is a simple reason for this. We have had years and years strewn with the litter of politicians promising to cut net migration to under 100,000 annually.

But it never happened, until now.

In the latter decades of the last century, net migration was broadly net zero. Sometimes more folk left than arrived. But, around the time that I first arrived as a reporter in Westminster in 2004, the story was changing and would change rapidly.

I have followed every twist, turn, argument and campaign since, both from Parliament and from Brussels.

On 1 May 2004, the European Union expanded hugely, from 15 to 25 members, the biggest expansion in its history.

The bloc's population grew by 74 million people overnight as countries including Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and what was then the Czech Republic signed up.

And remember, a core plank of EU membership is freedom of movement: the right to travel, live and work anywhere in the club.

Transitional controls on workers from these former communist states could be applied at the time, but the then-Labour government led by Tony Blair chose not to.

The consequences of that decision were as substantial as they were consequential.

Ministers had predicted a minimal impact. But net migration cranked up.

Crucially, this began to ground arguments about sovereignty in the swirling debates about the UK's membership of the EU.

At the time I was a Europe correspondent based in Brussels and a frequent visitor to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage, were on the rise. But Eurosceptics would tell me privately that their deeply held concerns about the loss of sovereignty, of power, to EU institutions had been a hard sell to many back home. It was an argument, regardless of its merits or otherwise, that felt theoretical and intellectual to many, rather than practical and grounded in day-to-day concerns.

But that changed for many given the scale of immigration people could see.

Plenty of places, particularly beyond the big cities, felt the rapidity of change. Immigration took on a greater political salience.

Should all control over migration be re-imported to Westminster? Such was the growing strength of feeling among many, a sequence of prime ministers began promising to reduce net migration to the tens of thousands.

David Cameron made the promise. The Conservative election manifesto in 2010 harked back to those numbers before the turn of the century. "We will take steps to take net migration back to the levels of the 1990s â tens of thousands a year, not hundreds of thousands."

Five years later, Cameron renewed the promise, in the Conservative manifesto of 2015. The party would "keep our ambition of delivering annual net migration in the tens of thousands, not the hundreds of thousands," it read.

By 2017, Theresa May was prime minister and while the UK had voted for Brexit, it hadn't happened yet. In the Conservative manifesto that year, she promised "controlled, sustainable migration, with net migration down to the tens of thousands."

At the 2019 general election, Boris Johnson was in Downing Street. He didn't repeat the tens of thousands promise, post Brexit, instead arguing for an "Australian-style points-based immigration system" and, crucially, that "overall numbers will come down."

They didn't. Instead, they soared by almost a million â a giant spike on the graph of recent net migration, branded by his critics as the "Boriswave."

Johnson argued that Brexit would mean Westminster would take back control of migration, as leaving the European Union would mean the end of freedom of movement among the member states.

And yes, Brexit did repatriate that power. But this delivered choices, not a guaranteed outcome that the numbers would fall. And Johnson's choices led instead to a spectacular rise.

It took Rishi Sunak's government and the then-Home Secretary Sir James Cleverly to substantially change the rules and so limit the number of visas granted. The incoming Labour government in 2024 inherited these rules and kept them.

The question now, with the net migration number now in the tens of thousands, is whether immigration will now shrivel as a topic of widespread worry.

How migration feels can be influenced by world view and wealth, politics and geography. Let's take just one aspect of it: the number of asylum seekers being housed in Scotland has increased by 20% over the past year, despite a fall in numbers across the UK as a whole. Glasgow remains the council area with the largest number of people in asylum accommodation in the UK, and there have been increases in areas from Aberdeen to North Lanarkshire which buck the UK-wide trend.

And a lower net figure also does not necessarily mean that the scale of immigration and emigration are low. Large but similar numbers merely serve to almost cancel each other out, numerically. The underlying official statistics set out that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June, while 661,000 emigrated.

But just as previous political choices still have consequences now, a persistently low net migration number, depending on who is coming and going, could have consequences in the future. Take Andy Burnham's desire to shake up social care in England, a sector traditionally reliant on arrivals from overseas for much of its workforce. How might it cope? It's one of many potential questions for the future.…
